# SSNAC IV: Measurement {#sec-data}

::: {#leading}
We describe the process of designing and testing a novel survey
questionnaire tool we call the MPX NYC person-place mapper. We show the
questions participants were presented with in the survey.
:::

## Person–Place Network Mapper

We designed, tested, and implemented the MPX NYC Person–Place Network
Mapper to address practical and ethical challenges in collecting
sensitive spatial data in an anonymous survey. Our aim was to capture
information on venues participants visited, including those where group
sex occurred, while minimizing the risk of re-identification through
location data.

### Place Mapping

Because participants were unlikely to recall precise addresses or zip
codes, we used the Google Maps API to let them identify locations by
landmarks, cross-streets, subway stations, and neighborhood names. The
map displayed detailed geographic information with standard navigation
tools (see Figure D.1).

Participants were prompted to identify specific types of places, such as
their primary residence, and then to select additional locations where
they had physical or sexual contact in group settings. Each tap on the
map placed a marker, which triggered follow-up questions about activity
at that site and the type of venue.

![Map input question format developed for MPX
NYC](../_const/images/image_app_graphic.png){#fig-mapinputformat}

### Link Tracing

We developed a referral system to build a network anonymously. At the
start of the survey, participants received a unique identifier card
containing a QR code and word combination, which they were asked to
save.

At the end of the survey, participants could share a pre-written
invitation with a unique URL. If a contact used the link, an edge was
added between the two respondents in the graph database. When a new
participant connected with someone who had already completed the survey,
the existing participant could confirm their identifier card, allowing
the system to link their nodes without revealing identities.

![Surey share dialogue](/_const/images/share_screen.png)

### Implementation

To reduce re-identification risk, spatial data were coarsened before
storage. For example, coordinates were converted to census tract
identifiers, preventing disclosure of exact locations such as a
dormitory or government office.

The tool’s front end was built as a single-page React/NextJS application
hosted on Vercel, with design based on the MPX NYC style guide. The back
end used a custom Neo4j graph database. Standard survey formats
(multiple choice, text, etc.) were integrated alongside the mapping and
referral components.

Data flow proceeded as follows: the front end loaded questions from a
JSON file, parsed referral identifiers and language settings from the
URL, and requested a public identifier from the API. The API generated
and stored public/private identifier pairs in a secure table, returned
the public identifier and QR code to the participant, and transformed
identifiers before sending responses to the graph database.

For spatial inputs, the front end queried the FCC API, which returned
census block identifiers. These were truncated to census tract
identifiers before being stored in the study database. Two rounds of
user testing with about ten participants each informed refinements to
usability and clarity.

RESPND-MI Web Application Requirements (Narrative) Flowchart Available
at: https://miro.com/app/board/uXjVOxeP sls=/?share_link_id=384361467333

We want to design a web app which: a) Collects self-reported health and
demographic information b) Maps out social and sexual networks The app
must not collect any identifying information from the user. This
includes name, email, phone number, ip address. For the user, there are
two pathways to the app: Either you find the link in an ad (scenario 1),
or you receive the link from a friend / sexual partner who has sent it
to you (scenario 2). Scenario 1: 1. User goes to the webpage (through
URL or barcode) 2. User is asked if they have participated in study
before. 3. If not, presented information about the study and asked if
they consent to participate 4. If they consent, they are presented with
a unique ID and prompted to save / screenshot it. (a button that helps
do this would be great) 5. they are asked some questions about their
demographics, behaviour, and health 6. When they have completed the
survey, they are asked to recall their sexual partners over the past X
weeks. 7. They are presented with a text which contains a URL that they
are prompted to send to those partners by copying it from the webpage
and pasting it into the message. They can use any method to send the
text. (have buttons that open and pre-populate imessenger, whatsapp,
sms, facebook messenger, twitter message ) 8. They are then asked to
recall the people they were in close contact with, but who they didnt
have sex with. 9. They are presented with a text as in point 7. 10. They
are finally asked if there are friends they have not seen in person that
they want to share the study with 11. They are presented with a text as
in point 7.

This is what would happen in the second scenario: 1. User receives text
from friend 2. User navigates to the page, and is asked if he has
participated in the study already 3. If they say yes: a. They are asked
for their unique ID 4. If they say no: a. They follow the steps from the
first scenario''
